script: A pilot hijacked his own passenger plane just to escape his home country. On February 17, 2014, Flight 702 took off from Addis Ababa with 202 people on board. While the captain stepped away, the co-pilot locked the cockpit door from the inside. He radioed a fuel emergency, then forced the plane toward Switzerland, alone in the cockpit, seeking asylum. Fighter jets scrambled to intercept him over Geneva, but they were French and Italian, not Swiss. Switzerland's own air force only works business hours. He landed the plane himself, climbed out the cockpit window on a rope, and surrendered. All two hundred and two people aboard were unharmed. Here's the part almost nobody expects. Switzerland never sent him to prison. Experts found he had been in a state of complete paranoia during the hijacking, so prosecutors dropped the case and ordered psychiatric treatment instead. It took Switzerland almost seven years to fix its airspace gap. Follow for more true stories nobody could make up.

metadata.title: Random But True: The Pilot Switzerland Couldn't Catch
metadata.caption:
On February 17, 2014, a co-pilot locked himself into the cockpit of Ethiopian Airlines Flight 702 and radioed a fuel emergency to divert the plane to Geneva, alone in the cockpit, seeking asylum.

Fighter jets scrambled to intercept him, but they were French and Italian, because Switzerland's own air force only operates business hours, and this happened before dawn on a Monday.

He landed the plane himself and climbed down a rope from the cockpit window to surrender. All 202 people on board walked away unharmed.

And here's the part almost nobody expects: Switzerland never sent him to prison. Experts found he had been in a state of complete paranoia during the hijacking, so prosecutors dropped the criminal case entirely.

It took Switzerland almost seven years to actually fix the airspace gap. Follow for more true stories nobody could make up.
